etymology: Hebrew Elitsur (H468), my God is a rock — from El (H410), God, and tsur (H6697), a rock, a cliff, a stronghold. The name is a confession before it is a label.
biblical_def: Elizur the son of Shedeur was the prince of the tribe of Reuben during the wilderness years, named by the LORD Himself when Moses was commanded to number the people: “of the tribe of Reuben; Elizur the son of Shedeur” (Num 1:5). He appears four times and always in the same office. He stands with Moses and Aaron at the census. He is captain over Reuben's camp on the south side of the tabernacle (Num 2:10). He brings his tribe's offering on the fourth day of the twelve-day dedication (Num 7:30). He leads Reuben's host when the camp sets forward (Num 10:18). Scripture tells us nothing else about him — no speech, no failure, no exploit. What it tells us is his name, and his name is a sermon: my God is a rock. Reuben was the firstborn who lost the birthright by instability, unstable as water (Gen 49:4); and the man set over Reuben's thousands carries in his name the opposite of water. A tribe that forfeited its place through inconstancy is led by a man called my God is a rock. That is not accident. It is the LORD's habit of preaching through the ordinary, and of giving a people the very word they most need to hear spoken over them every time the captain is called by name.
webster_summary: The prince of the tribe of Reuben in the wilderness, son of Shedeur; his name means my God is a rock.

corruption_summary: Modern criticism files the wilderness name-lists as invented administrative fiction; they are the register of a real people whom God numbered by name.
corruption_paragraphs: The lists of Numbers 1, 2, 7 and 10 are the standard exhibit for the claim that the Pentateuch's census material is late bureaucratic invention — the documentary hypothesis assigns them to a priestly source writing centuries after Moses, on the reasoning that no wilderness generation would have kept such records. The reasoning assumes what it means to prove. Moses was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Act 7:22), and Egypt kept muster rolls; a nation marching in ordered ranks with a sanctuary at its centre is precisely the sort of body that keeps a list. More to the point, the text presents these names as the LORD's own designation — these are the names of the men that shall stand with you — and the dictionary takes Moses at his word, because the Lord Jesus did (Joh 5:46-47).

The second corruption is quieter and commoner among believers: the habit of skipping the name-lists as though they were filler between the interesting parts. They are not filler. They are the proof that the God who saves saves particular people, and that He knows them one at a time. Elizur is not a number in Reuben's column; he is the man the LORD named to stand beside Moses. The same God writes names in the book of life (Rev 20:15) and calls His own sheep by name (Joh 10:3). A reader who learns to slow down at a wilderness roll has learned something about how he himself is known.

etymology: Hebrew Shedeyur (H7707), commonly read as caster forth of light or the Almighty is light — joining Shaddai (H7706), the Almighty, to ur (H217), flame or light.
biblical_def: Shedeur is known to Scripture only as a father. Five times the wilderness record names him, and every time in the same construction: Elizur the son of Shedeur (Num 1:5; 2:10; 7:30, 35; 10:18). He is of the tribe of Reuben, and he never speaks, acts, or is numbered in his own right. That is worth pausing over. The generation that came out of Egypt fell in the wilderness for unbelief (Heb 3:17-19), and Shedeur was of that generation; the son stands at the head of the tribe while the father's whole record is the single word son of. Yet the record is not nothing. Israel reckoned every prince by his father's house — heads of the house of their fathers (Num 7:2) — and a man whose name is attached to the captain of Reuben in four separate chapters has left a real mark on the covenant people. The name itself carries light: Shaddai is light. Set beside his son's name, my God is a rock, the pair reads as a household confession handed down — light from the father, refuge from the son. Israelite naming was catechesis, and a family that named its sons this way was teaching the next generation who God is before that generation could speak.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fatherhood is a real office whose fruit outlives the record of the father.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No movement has any interest in Shedeur. What presses on a modern reader instead is the smallness of the record — a man remembered only as somebody's father — and the instinct to count that a waste. Our age measures a life by what it accomplishes under its own name, and a man whose entire scriptural footprint is the phrase son of Shedeur looks, by that measure, like nothing at all.

Scripture measures otherwise. The command to fathers is to teach the words of God diligently unto their children, talking of them when they sit in the house and when they walk by the way (Deu 6:7), and the fruit of that work usually appears under another man's name. Shedeur raised a son whom the LORD named to stand beside Moses. Timothy's faith dwelt first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2Ti 1:5), and it is Timothy's name on the epistle. The principle to recover is that the ordinary, unrecorded labour of a godly household is not a lesser kind of service; it is the ordinary means by which God supplies the next generation's leaders.

etymology: Hebrew Shelumiel (H8017), God is my peace — from shalom (H7965), peace, wholeness, welfare, and El (H410), God.
biblical_def: Shelumiel the son of Zurishaddai was prince and captain of the tribe of Simeon through the wilderness years. The LORD named him to stand with Moses at the numbering (Num 1:6); he commanded Simeon's camp, pitched next to Reuben on the south (Num 2:12); he brought his tribe's offering on the fifth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:36); and he led Simeon's host when the standards moved (Num 10:19). As with the other princes, Scripture records no word of his and no deed beyond his office, and as with the others the name itself is the message: God is my peace. Simeon needed that word. Simeon and Levi were the brothers of cruelty whose anger Jacob cursed — I will divide them in Jacob, and scatter them in Israel (Gen 49:7) — and Simeon's later history in the wilderness is grim, for it was a prince of Simeon who brought a Midianitish woman into the camp and fell under Phinehas' javelin (Num 25:14). Over a tribe marked by violence and by the sin at Peor stands a captain whose name confesses that peace is not achieved but received: God is my peace. The whole gospel is compressed in the grammar. Peace is not a thing Simeon makes; it is a Person Simeon has.

corruption_summary: Peace is now treated as a mood to be managed; the name confesses it as a gift held in God Himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern use of peace has shrunk to an inward state — calm, balance, the absence of stress — and the means offered for it are techniques. Scripture's peace is first a standing, not a feeling: being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Rom 5:1). The war is real, the enmity is real, and it is ended by blood, not by breathing. Only after the standing is settled does the experience follow, and even then it is guarded by God rather than generated by the believer — the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus (Php 4:7). Shelumiel's name has the order right: God is my peace, not I have found my peace.

The second thing to recover is that this peace was spoken over a tribe with a violent record. Simeon's name is attached to Shechem's slaughter and to the sin at Peor, and yet the captain the LORD sets over Simeon carries a confession of peace. Grace habitually does this — it names a people by what God is toward them rather than by what they have been. The church is called saints while it is still being sanctified, beloved while it is still being corrected. To hear Shelumiel called out at every muster was to hear Simeon told, again, that its hope lay outside itself.

etymology: Hebrew Tsurishadday (H6701), my rock is the Almighty — from tsur (H6697), rock, and Shaddai (H7706), the Almighty.
biblical_def: Zurishaddai was a man of the tribe of Simeon in the generation of the exodus, and Scripture names him five times, always as the father of Shelumiel the prince of Simeon (Num 1:6; 2:12; 7:36, 41; 10:19). Like Shedeur of Reuben he has no recorded word or act of his own. What he has is a name that states a doctrine outright: my rock is the Almighty. Both halves matter. Tsur, rock, is the covenant title of God in the Song of Moses, where it is pressed six times over — He is the Rock, his work is perfect: for all his ways are judgment (Deu 32:4). Shaddai, the Almighty, is the name by which God made Himself known to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob before the name Jehovah was declared to Moses (Exo 6:3). So the name binds together the patriarchal revelation and the wilderness confession, and it puts them in the first person singular: not the Almighty is a rock, but my rock is the Almighty. That possessive is the difference between doctrine held and doctrine trusted. Father and son together confess the whole of it — the father, that the Almighty is his refuge; the son, that God is his peace. Refuge first, then peace: the order in which a soul actually receives them.

corruption_summary: God as rock is softened into a figure for personal resilience; Scripture means an immovable Person outside the self.
corruption_paragraphs: The rock language of Scripture is regularly borrowed for a doctrine it contradicts — the idea that a man must find the bedrock within himself, that strength is discovered by looking inward and holding steady. Every biblical use points the other way. The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust (Psa 18:2). A rock is valuable precisely because it is not the man: it does not move when he moves, does not fail when he fails, and can be stood upon when he has no standing of his own. Zurishaddai's name locates the rock outside himself and above himself, and calls it Almighty.

The second recovery is the possessive. My rock is the Almighty. Scripture is full of men who knew the doctrine and perished for want of the pronoun; the wilderness generation heard the truth and it did not profit them, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it (Heb 4:2). Sound theology held at arm's length saves nobody. What the name of a Simeonite father models is the personal appropriation the confessions call saving faith — not merely assenting that God is a rock, but resting the whole weight of one's soul on Him as mine.

etymology: Hebrew Tsuar (H6686), littleness or smallness — from the root tsaar (H6819), to be small, to be brought low.
biblical_def: Zuar was a man of the tribe of Issachar in the wilderness generation, named five times in Numbers and always as the father of Nethaneel, prince of Issachar (Num 1:8; 2:5; 7:18, 23; 10:15). His name means littleness. Israelite names were given in earnest, and a father called small stands at the head of a house whose son was made captain over more than fifty thousand men. Issachar's place in the order of march was near the front, pitched on the east beside Judah, and Nethaneel offered on the second day of the dedication — second only to Judah itself. The smallness in the name and the prominence in the office are not in conflict; they are the pattern by which God habitually works. God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty (1Co 1:27). Gideon was the least in his father's house; David was the youngest son, keeping sheep; Bethlehem was little among the thousands of Judah, and out of it came the Ruler of Israel (Mic 5:2). A tribe led by the son of a man named little was being taught, every time the roll was called, that greatness in Israel is a thing conferred and not a thing possessed.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God exalts the low and that smallness is no barrier to usefulness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Zuar is too obscure to have attracted any revision. The live temptation is the one his name rebukes: the assumption that a person's usefulness to God scales with his visibility, and that a small life is a wasted one. Our age has made a virtue of scale and a shame of obscurity, and believers absorb it — measuring ministry by audience, fruitfulness by reach, faithfulness by platform.

Scripture reverses the measure without apology. He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree (Luk 1:52). The Lord Jesus was Himself of no reputation (Php 2:7), and the kingdom He preached belongs to the poor in spirit. The principle to recover is that God is not embarrassed by small things and does not need large ones: He fed a multitude from a boy's five loaves, built His church on fishermen, and set the son of a man named little over the host of Issachar. A believer who learns this stops apologising for the size of his life and gets on with the work in front of him.

etymology: Hebrew Chelon (H2497), commonly read as strong or full of hope, from a root akin to chayil (H2428), strength, valour, an army in force.
biblical_def: Helon was a man of the tribe of Zebulun in the exodus generation, named five times in the book of Numbers and never apart from his son: Eliab the son of Helon (Num 1:9; 2:7; 7:24, 29; 10:16). Eliab was prince and captain of Zebulun, pitched on the east with Judah and Issachar, offering on the third day of the altar's dedication and leading Zebulun's host at the setting forward of the camp. Helon himself is a name and a lineage and nothing more. The name carries the idea of strength — of a man of force, of a household with substance in it. Zebulun was the tribe Moses blessed with the words Rejoice, Zebulun, in thy going out (Deu 33:18), a seafaring, venturing people; and Deborah's song remembers that out of Zebulun came they that handle the pen of the writer (Jdg 5:14) and men who jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field (Jdg 5:18). It is a fitting house from which to draw a captain, and a fitting father's name to stand behind him. Scripture's reticence about Helon is not neglect. It is the ordinary shape of covenant faithfulness, which is usually transmitted rather than recorded.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that strength in Scripture is given for service, not for display.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nothing in the modern academy or the modern church has any quarrel with Helon. The word his name carries, however, is contested constantly. Strength in current usage is either a therapeutic virtue — the capacity to endure and self-soothe — or a matter of dominance and self-assertion. Both readings make strength a possession to be measured and shown.

The biblical account of strength is that it is loaned for a purpose. The LORD is my strength and my shield (Psa 28:7); my strength is made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9); the men of Zebulun were strong and they spent it jeoparding their lives in the high places of the field for the people of God. The principle to recover is stewardship: a strong man in Scripture is a man with more to spend on others, not more to keep for himself. Where strength turns inward it becomes the thing Scripture calls the arm of flesh, and cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm (Jer 17:5).

etymology: Hebrew Pedahtsur (H6301), the rock has ransomed — from padah (H6299), to ransom, to redeem by paying a price, and tsur (H6697), rock.
biblical_def: Pedahzur was of the tribe of Manasseh in the wilderness generation, and Scripture names him five times as the father of Gamaliel, prince and captain of Manasseh (Num 1:10; 2:20; 7:54, 59; 10:23). Manasseh camped on the west with Ephraim and Benjamin, and Gamaliel offered on the eighth day of the twelve-day dedication of the altar. Of Pedahzur himself nothing further is told. His name, however, is among the most doctrinally loaded in the entire wilderness roll: the rock has ransomed. Padah is the verb of the redemption price — the word used when the firstborn of Israel are bought back with silver (Num 18:15-16), and the word David uses of his own soul: God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave (Psa 49:15). Joined to tsur, the covenant title of God as Rock, it makes a complete sentence of gospel: the unmovable God has paid a price and bought His people out. A man of the generation redeemed out of Egypt by the blood of a lamb carried that sentence as his name, and his son commanded a tribe under it. Every muster of Manasseh was, without anyone intending it, a rehearsal of the doctrine of redemption by purchase.

And over the host of the tribe of the children of Manasseh was Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur.
corruption_summary: Redemption is emptied into a metaphor for self-improvement; the Hebrew verb in this name means a price was actually paid.
corruption_paragraphs: To redeem in modern speech means to make up for a failure — a redeeming quality, a redemption arc, a man redeeming himself by later good conduct. The subject of the verb is the one who failed, and the currency is his own subsequent performance. Scripture never once uses the word that way. In padah and its New Testament counterparts the subject is always the deliverer, never the captive, and the currency is always a price paid by another. The firstborn of Israel did not redeem themselves; they were bought with five shekels. Israel did not redeem herself from Egypt; the LORD hath redeemed you out of the house of bondmen (Deu 7:8).

The price is the offence and the glory of the doctrine. Ye are not your own, for ye are bought with a price (1Co 6:19-20); ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold… but with the precious blood of Christ (1Pe 1:18-19). Pedahzur's name puts the payer beyond mistaking: it is the Rock who ransoms. Any account of salvation in which the sinner contributes the purchase price has abandoned the word, and with it the only ground on which a guilty man may stand.
roots_summary: Hebrew Pedahtsur (H6301), from padah (H6299), to ransom by paying a price, and tsur (H6697), rock.
roots_lines: Hebrew padah (H6299) — to ransom, to redeem by payment; used of the firstborn bought back with silver (Num 18:15-16).

“The rock has ransomed” — the doctrine of purchase carried in a wilderness name.

etymology: Hebrew Gidoni (H1441), my cutter down or hewer — from gada (H1438), to cut down, to hew asunder, the verb used of felling the groves and hewing down the altars of idolatry.
biblical_def: Gideoni was a man of the tribe of Benjamin in the exodus generation, named five times in Numbers as the father of Abidan, prince and captain of Benjamin (Num 1:11; 2:22; 7:60, 65; 10:24). Benjamin pitched on the west with Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Rachel keeping together; Abidan offered on the ninth day of the dedication and led Benjamin's host at the setting forward. Gideoni's own record is his name and his son. The name comes from gada, to hew down — the same verb that stands behind Gideon's name and behind the standing command to Israel concerning the idolatry of Canaan: ye shall destroy their altars, and break their images, and cut down their groves (Exo 34:13). It is a name of demolition, and it belongs to the covenant. Before Israel could build, Israel had to cut down; the land was to be cleared of its high places before the tabernacle had a settled home in it. A father named hewer at the head of a Benjamite house was a standing reminder that the LORD's people are called not only to worship rightly but to tear out what competes with right worship, beginning at home.
webster_summary: A Benjamite of the exodus generation, father of Abidan prince of Benjamin; his name means hewer or my cutter down.
webster_full: GIDEONI, Hebrew Gidoni, my cutter down, hewer.

From gada, to cut down, the verb used of hewing down idolatrous groves.

corruption_summary: The demolition side of repentance is treated as harshness; Scripture makes cutting down the necessary first half of covenant obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: A church shaped by the therapeutic mood wants building without breaking. Repentance is recast as growth, sin as a pattern to be gently outgrown, and any language of cutting, mortifying or destroying is felt to be violent and unkind. Scripture is unembarrassed about it. The command at Sinai was to break the images and cut down the groves; the Lord Jesus spoke of cutting off the hand and plucking out the eye (Mat 5:29-30); and Paul wrote to the saints at Colosse, mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth (Col 3:5). Mortify means put to death. There is no softer word for it in the text.

Owen's maxim stands: be killing sin, or it will be killing you. The reason the demolition is required is that the ground is not empty. An idol does not vacate the heart because something better has been introduced alongside it; the groves must come down before the tabernacle is at home in the land. The principle to recover from a Benjamite named hewer is that mortification is not an optional severity for the unusually rigorous believer but the ordinary daily work of everyone who has been made alive, and that a gospel offering only comfort and never the axe is not the gospel the apostles preached.

etymology: Hebrew Pagiel (H6295), God meets or God intervenes — from paga (H6293), to meet, to encounter, to fall upon, to intercede, and El (H410), God.
biblical_def: Pagiel the son of Ocran was prince and captain of the tribe of Asher through the wilderness years. He was named by the LORD to stand with Moses at the numbering (Num 1:13), commanded Asher's camp on the north side beside Dan and Naphtali (Num 2:27), brought his tribe's offering on the eleventh day of the dedication (Num 7:72), and led Asher's host when the standards went forward (Num 10:26). Scripture gives him no speech and no deed apart from his office. His name means God meets, from paga — a verb of encounter that runs the whole range from a chance meeting on a road to a violent falling upon an enemy, and then rises to its highest use in Isaiah, where it is the word for intercession: he made intercession for the transgressors (Isa 53:12), and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all (Isa 53:6), where the verb is the same — our iniquity was made to meet upon Him. Asher was the tribe blessed with fatness and oil, let him dip his foot in oil (Deu 33:24), the most comfortable portion in Israel; and over that comfortable tribe stood a captain whose name said that God is not distant but comes to meet His people.
webster_summary: Prince and captain of the tribe of Asher in the wilderness, son of Ocran; his name means God meets.
webster_full: PAGIEL, Hebrew Pagiel, God meets, or God intervenes.

corruption_summary: God is imagined as waiting to be found by the seeker; the verb in this name has Him doing the meeting.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern religious language is built around the seeker. Men are said to be on a journey, searching for God, encountering the divine on their own terms and in their own time. Scripture's account is the reverse at every point. There is none that seeketh after God (Rom 3:11); the Son of man came to seek and to save that which was lost (Luk 19:10); the shepherd goes after the one sheep until he finds it. Where men do seek, it is because they have first been sought — ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you (Joh 15:16). Pagiel's name keeps the subject of the verb in its right place: God meets.

The verb rises higher still. Paga is Isaiah's word for intercession, and in the fifty-third chapter it carries the very transaction of the atonement: the LORD made our iniquity to meet upon the Servant, and the Servant made intercession for transgressors. The meeting God arranges is therefore not a warm encounter but a substitution — our sin meeting Him, His righteousness meeting us. Any spirituality that speaks of meeting God while leaving out the place where sin was made to meet Christ has not found the God of Israel but an idol of the same name.

Hebrew El (H410) — God, the Mighty One; the divine element of the name.

etymology: Hebrew Okran (H5918), troubler or troubled — from akar (H5916), to trouble, to stir up as muddy water, to bring calamity upon.
biblical_def: Ocran was a man of the tribe of Asher in the wilderness generation, named five times in Numbers as the father of Pagiel, prince of Asher (Num 1:13; 2:27; 7:72, 77; 10:26). Nothing else is recorded of him. His name comes from akar, to trouble — the verb of Achan, whose sin brought calamity on the camp and gave the valley of Achor its name (Jos 7:25-26), and the verb Ahab flung at Elijah, Art thou he that troubleth Israel? (1Ki 18:17). It is a dark word to carry, and the contrast with his son's name is the whole point of the pair: Ocran, trouble; Pagiel, God meets. Read together, father and son state the gospel order — trouble first, and then God coming to meet the troubled. Elijah's answer to Ahab made the same correction: I have not troubled Israel; but thou, and thy father's house (1Ki 18:18). Trouble in Scripture is rarely arbitrary; it is either the fruit of sin or the instrument by which God brings a people to the place of meeting. Hosea promised that the LORD would give Israel the valley of Achor for a door of hope (Hos 2:15) — the very valley of trouble turned into an entrance.
webster_summary: A man of Asher in the wilderness generation, father of Pagiel prince of Asher; his name means troubler.
webster_full: OCRAN, Hebrew Okran, troubler, or troubled.

From akar, to trouble, to stir up as muddy water; the verb of Achan and of the valley of Achor.

corruption_summary: Trouble is treated as a problem to be eliminated; Scripture treats it as either the wages of sin or the door of hope.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct before trouble is to explain it away or engineer it out — to treat every affliction as a malfunction and every sufferer as a person owed relief. Scripture is more sober and more hopeful at once. It knows trouble that is judicial, the direct harvest of sin: Achan troubled the camp and the camp buried him in the valley that took his name. It knows trouble that is disciplinary: before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word (Psa 119:67). And it knows trouble that is simply the weather of a fallen world, which the Lord Jesus promised outright — in the world ye shall have tribulation (Joh 16:33).

What Scripture never does is leave trouble as the last word. The same valley of Achor that swallowed Achan is promised back as a door of hope (Hos 2:15); the light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory (2Co 4:17). A father named trouble whose son is named God meets has the sequence right, and the principle to recover is that the Christian is not promised a life without trouble but a God who comes into it.
